Argentine Banking Sector Faces Disruption as Workers Stage Nationwide Walkout

Banking operations across Argentina have been hit by a large-scale walkout, now in its second day, as thousands of banking employees protest wage conditions and seek improved benefits. The action, led by the National Union of Bank Workers (NUBW), has resulted in the closure of the majority of bank branches and service offices nationwide.

The strike began early Tuesday morning after overnight negotiations between the union and the Argentine Banking Association (ABA) failed to produce a new wage agreement. “Our members are demanding fair compensation in line with rising inflation and the increased cost of living,” stated NUBW General Secretary Mariano Gutiérrez in a press conference outside the organization’s Buenos Aires headquarters. “Until meaningful progress is made, we will continue with industrial action.”

Industry sources estimate that more than 80 percent of branch locations operated by major banking groups such as Banco del Plata and SolFin Bancaria remain closed. Many employees have joined picket lines in central districts of major cities, while others have participated in organized assemblies at regional offices. Digital banking services are reported to be operating intermittently, as technical staff and call center workers have also joined the walkout in significant numbers.

The ABA expressed concern about the mounting disruptions. “The ongoing strike is impacting our ability to provide essential banking services to customers and to maintain regular financial operations,” said ABA spokesperson Lucía Fernández. “We are urging all parties to return to the negotiating table in the interest of sector stability.”

With talks at a standstill, the union has signaled that the walkout could be extended if their demands are not met. Analysts within the industry warn that a prolonged strike could further affect banking operations and staff morale. At the time of writing, both sides have yet to confirm a date for renewed negotiations.
